title: The Planck length
fact: The scale where our theories of space and time are expected to break down. Inflate a banana to the size of the observable universe and a Planck length would grow to about 70 nanometres — roughly the size of a virus.

title: Uncharted territory
fact: Between the smallest things ever measured and the Planck length lie some 16 orders of magnitude that no experiment has touched. Grand unified theories place new physics around 10⁻³² m, but nobody knows what is really down here.

title: Quarks and electrons
fact: Electrons and quarks show no measurable size at all: collider experiments say they are smaller than about 10⁻¹⁹ m, if they have a size. Physics treats them as points.

title: A proton
fact: Three quarks bound by gluons — yet the quarks' own masses add up to only about 1% of the proton's. The rest is the energy of the strong force itself, turned into mass via E = mc².

title: A potassium-40 nucleus
fact: 19 protons and 21 neutrons. A banana holds about 50 micrograms of potassium-40, and roughly 15 of these nuclei decay inside it every second. Your banana is (very mildly) radioactive.

title: A potassium atom
fact: Scale the nucleus up to a pea and the electron cloud would fill a football stadium. More than 99.9999999999% of an atom's volume is empty space — which is why the scroll from here to the nucleus is so dark.

title: The DNA double helix
fact: Two nanometres wide, yet the DNA in a single one of your cells would stretch about two metres if uncoiled. The popular claim that we share 60% of our DNA with bananas really refers to shared gene families, not identical code.

title: A ribosome
fact: The protein factory of every living cell: it reads a messenger RNA and chains amino acids together, several per second. Each of your cells contains up to ten million of them.

title: A coronavirus
fact: About 100 nanometres across — smaller than the wavelength of visible light (400–700 nm), which is why no ordinary light microscope can show you one. This is a medical illustration, not a photograph.

title: E. coli bacteria
fact: In ideal conditions E. coli divides every 20 minutes. Your gut hosts about as many bacterial cells as your body has human cells: tens of trillions of each.

title: Red blood cells
fact: You make more than two million every second. They have no nucleus — they are bags of haemoglobin that fold to squeeze through capillaries narrower than themselves. The white blob is a white blood cell.

title: Pollen grains
fact: Pollen walls are made of sporopollenin, one of the toughest organic materials known. Grains survive in lake sediments for millions of years, letting scientists reconstruct ancient climates. Colours are added; electron microscopes see in greyscale.

title: A tardigrade
fact: Half a millimetre of near-indestructibility. Tardigrades survive drying out, near-absolute-zero cold and the vacuum of space: in 2007 some rode outside a satellite and revived back on Earth.

visual.commons: SEM image of Milnesium tardigradum in active state - journal.pone.0045682.g001-2.png

title: A honey bee
fact: Foragers tell their sisters where flowers are with the waggle dance: the angle of the dance encodes the direction relative to the Sun, its duration the distance. Karl von Frisch shared a Nobel Prize for decoding it.

title: A banana
fact: Botanically a berry, mildly radioactive, and the internet's favourite unit of length. Almost every banana exported worldwide is a Cavendish: a sterile clone, genetically identical to all the others.

title: A human
fact: On a logarithmic scale we are not in the middle of things: halfway between the Planck length and the observable universe sits about 0.1 mm — the width of a hair, or a tardigrade.

title: A blue whale
fact: Up to 30 metres and over 150 tonnes: the heaviest animal known to have ever lived, dinosaurs included. Its low-frequency calls can carry for hundreds of kilometres through the ocean.

title: A Saturn V rocket
fact: 111 metres of rocket that sent humans to the Moon. Its first stage burned about 13 tonnes of propellant every second for two and a half minutes.

title: The Burj Khalifa
fact: 828 metres, the tallest building in the world since 2010. From the top the horizon is about 100 km away.

title: Mount Everest
fact: 8,849 metres above sea level — but its summit is not the point farthest from Earth's centre. That is Chimborazo in Ecuador, lifted by the planet's equatorial bulge.

visual.commons: Everest North Face toward Base Camp Tibet Luca Galuzzi 2006.jpg

title: A hurricane
fact: Hurricane Isabel, photographed from the International Space Station in 2003. A mature hurricane releases heat from condensing rain at a rate around 200 times humanity's entire electricity generating capacity.

title: The Moon
fact: It drifts away from us by about 3.8 cm a year, as tides slowly hand Earth's spin over to the Moon's orbit. Days on Earth are getting longer as a result.

title: Earth
fact: The Blue Marble, photographed by the Apollo 17 crew in 1972. Most of the atmosphere's mass lies within 16 km of the surface: relative to the planet it is far thinner than a banana's peel.

title: Jupiter
fact: More than twice as massive as all the other planets combined. The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been raging for at least 190 years.

visual.commons: Jupiter and its shrunken Great Red Spot.jpg

title: The Sun
fact: Its light reaches us in 8 minutes 20 seconds, but the energy it carries was made in the core and spent tens of thousands of years or more bouncing its way out to the surface.

title: The inner Solar System
fact: The orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, to scale. Venus is the hottest planet at about 465 °C — hotter than Mercury, which is closer to the Sun — thanks to a runaway greenhouse effect.

title: The planets
fact: Neptune's orbit, 60 AU across. Neptune takes 165 years to go round the Sun: it completed its first full orbit since its discovery only in 2011.

title: The heliosphere
fact: The bubble blown by the solar wind. Voyager 1, launched in 1977, crossed its edge in 2012 and is now about a light-day from Earth: a radio message takes 24 hours to reach it.

title: The Oort cloud
fact: A hypothesised shell of trillions of icy bodies, the source of long-period comets. Nobody has ever seen it directly: it is inferred from comet orbits. Its outer edge may reach a third of the way to the nearest star.

title: The Orion Nebula
fact: A stellar nursery 1,300 light-years away, visible to the naked eye in Orion's sword. Hubble found dozens of protoplanetary discs inside it: solar systems being born.

title: The Milky Way
fact: 100 to 400 billion stars. The Sun takes about 230 million years to circle the centre; the last time it was where it is now, the first dinosaurs were appearing. This is an artist's impression — no one can photograph our galaxy from outside.

visual.commons: Artist’s impression of the Milky Way.jpg

title: The Local Group
fact: More than 80 galaxies dominated by the Milky Way and Andromeda. Andromeda is approaching at about 110 km/s, but recent simulations give only about even odds that the two will merge in the next 10 billion years.

title: Laniakea supercluster
fact: Our home supercluster, mapped in 2014 by how galaxies move: about 100,000 of them flowing toward a region called the Great Attractor. Its name is Hawaiian for 'immeasurable heaven'.

title: The observable universe
fact: 93 billion light-years across, even though the universe is only 13.8 billion years old — space kept expanding while the light was travelling. This is the cosmic microwave background, the oldest light there is, mapped across the whole sky by NASA's WMAP.
